While Mark Carney is being fêted around the world for standing up to the bully next door, his ambassadors in Haiti, the last and his replacement, meddle deeply into that country's governance.

For instance, before he departed Haiti last summer, André François Giroux, Canada's previous ambassador to Haiti, stated with no irony that "Canada opted to support Prime Minister Alix Fils-Aimé as a mark of continuity."

The problem with that is that 1) Canada thus violates Article 2 of the UN Charter, which promotes "sovereign equality" and Article 41 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which mandates non interference in other countries' internal affairs ; 2) Haiti's presidency had fired the Prime Minister for "incompetence" but he refused to step down due to foreign support.

In no way did the Canadian ambassador have any ground to interfere. Yet Carney jaunts around the world preaching that "great powers" are bullying middle ones, which must coalesce to maintain their sovereignty. That's rather hypocritical, in addition to being over the top, from a man whose ambassador acts an overlord in a foreign country.

Thus, to many of us, Carney's loftiness is empty rethoric. It applies only to Europeans. In practice, Carney does not believe in a world characterised by equal sovereignty, except for countries like Canada. So, next time he pontificates, expressing indignation at Trump's overwrought behaviour, remember what his government has done and is still doing in Haiti.

When evaluating bridge strikes in the Russia-Ukraine war, international reporting must weigh a crucial strategic asymmetry. While the collapse of the Kerch Strait Bridge is a high-profile military setback and a major blow to Russian logistics and prestige in Crimea, it is not an existential threat to Moscow. As a massive continental power, Russia can absorb the disruption by rerouting supplies through its southern overland corridor or maritime routes, leaving the survival of the state untouched.
Conversely, systematic Russian targeting of critical interior crossings—such as the bridges spanning the Dnipro River—carries far more immediate and debilitating consequences. Because Ukraine is fighting a defensive war within a compressed national footprint, its internal logistics, troop movements, and civilian economic continuity depend entirely on a limited number of major river bridges. Compromising these lifelines threatens to fracture the functional cohesion of the country's defense in a way that isolated infrastructure strikes against Russia simply do not.
Western reporting naturally focuses heavily on the Kerch Bridge because of its political symbolism as a link cementing Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea. However, a fair assessment requires acknowledging that the scale of vulnerability is starkly unequal: for Russia, losing a bridge is a severe logistics and public relations crisis, whereas for Ukraine, losing core interior river crossings threatens national survival itself.

Their removal fosters thought in the silence created by the simple absence of ceaseless stimulation. Education is foundational to building the models of reality, which are the basis of life's most important decisions. Socialization and games both have their place in anyone's life, but making a device the core of both activities is restricted and actually reduces the positive impacts of both activities. Add something like Altman's irresponsibly coded ChatGTP into that mix, and you end up with something that fosters isolation from other people- and often enough, reality.  Screen time has its place- I'm enjoying some myself right now- but not in a classroom unless it's something like computer science, or searching for information as part of a project of some kind. Phones are tools. They can access an amazing depth of information- but most of us, as has already been said, use them to argue with strangers and look at pictures of cats.

The human cost of this transition is undeniable and heartbreaking. For children facing terminal illnesses, a delay in access to clinical trials can mean the loss of their only remaining hope. That deserves serious scrutiny and accountability.

But the broader facts matter, too. The NCI consolidated overlapping research networks, committed additional funding, and sought to expand access to clinical trials. Those are hardly the actions of an administration abandoning pediatric cancer research.

The legitimate question is whether this restructuring could have been accomplished without disrupting treatment opportunities for desperately ill children. That is a serious and important story. Framing it instead as “science under siege” obscures the real tragedy: vulnerable patients bearing the immediate costs of a reorganization intended to improve medical research for future generations.

Legal ethics actually constrain the longer-term cohesion of large firms.   

Legal ethics effectively prohibit non-compete agreements.  The principle is that clients choose their lawyers, and it isn't up to other lawyers to say to a client "sorry, you can't work with that guy" - or to a lawyer who resigns "Sorry, you are not allowed to work with that client."  

So a lawyer can always bring his or her relationships with them.  Theoretically they're not allowed to ask a client before they leave whether the client will join them at a new place, so sometimes, to their chagrin and regret, they can discover their client isn't really "theirs" either.   That tends to temper the excitement a bit.  But generally a departing partner has reason to think key clients, and key colleagues, will join them.

And they do, both within their team, and with their clients.

When we visited Stromness in 1992,  fur seals were living in the buildings, but the buildings themselves were intact. You could walk into the labs, where beakers were still lined up, filled with whale oil. In "South", Shackleton wrote  
‘When I look back at those days I have no doubt that Providence guided us, not only across those snowfields, but across the storm-white sea that separated Elephant Island from our landing-place on South Georgia.  I know that during that long and racking march of thirty-six hours over the unnamed mountains and glaciers of South Georgia it seemed to me often that we were four, not three.  I said nothing to my companions on the point, but afterwards Worsley said to me, “Boss, I had a curious feeling on the march that there was another person with us.”  
Crean confessed to the same idea.  One feels “the dearth of human words, the roughness of mortal speech”* in trying to describe things intangible, but a record of our journeys would be incomplete without a reference to a subject very near to our hearts.’

Which found its way into T.S. Eliot's "The Wasteland".

"Who is the third who walks always beside you?
When I count, there are only you and I together
But when I look ahead up the white road
There is always another one walking beside you
Gliding wrapt in a brown mantle, hooded

—But who is that on the other side of you?’

I hosted Howard once in my home in Chico in 2008.  He always stayed in a local activist's home rather than in a hotel, and he always appreciated staying with vegans. He had been invited to town to give a talk before a group of California State University Chico ag students -- 2nd, 3rd, and 4th generation ranchers and farmers. His ability to speak as a peer to this adversarial and hostile audience of ranchers was masterful -- these young people listened to him and he rebutted all their gotcha questions. 

He was tireless in his advocacy for change for the better for all of us - for the animals, for our health, and for the planet. He returned to Chico in 2018 to speak again at Chico State as part of a panel on Proposition 12 — The Prevention of Farm Animal Cruelty Act — the landmark voter initiative that set the foundation for California’s modern farm animal welfare that is still being fought by the ag industry to this day. Prop 12 passed with huge support - 67% of California voters voted yes.

My favorite motto of his was: 

"Farmers should be feeding people, not animals." 

which speaks so effectively to the fact that about 40% of global arable land is used to grow crops to feed animals, which doesn't even include land used for grazing.

His was a life well lived, with purpose, with kindness, with gentle persistence, and with compassion for our fellow earthlings.

I and my partner were in the audience seated a few rows behind where Phillip had descended from the stage.  My partner went up to him and he immediately recognized her from high school days, took her hand and gave it a kiss. comments.name: maryann

Scientists and IP attorneys need to think a little harder about this one. If the historical argument that data ( from zebrafish, mice or other organisms) belonged to the investigator, well, you don't own people in your study the way you own laboratory animals-- people have agency. Humans who participate in study should have certain rights beyond privacy.
You want to publish data from me in a scholarly forum?
Fine. 
You want to use it as the basis for obtaining another research grant? 
Fine. 
You want to patent it and then use it in your start up that you sell for $500 million ( thank you, ma'am!)?
No.
You want to use it to harm others, or for other nefarious purposes? 
No.
I"m not sure how many people have ever sued about a participation agreement, but it would be interesting to see how many of these draconian clauses would actually hold up in court. I mean real court, not the paid IRB discussion panel.

Don't invest in what you don't understand!

I avoided the 2008 financial disaster by parking my remaining 401K funds into FDIC IRA CD's. I later got back into the market with another employer 401k. Not long ago I began moving all of it into High Yield FDIC IRA CD's now around 4%+. This is not a get rich quick plan, it's a retirement age wealth protection plan. I mostly hold 1-2-yr term CD's. It looks very likely yields will rise when the Fed starts raising rates higher next month. I just funded a 4.5% IRA CD, I expect 5% offers in early-mid 2027. 

I have no risk tolerance and little time horizon to recover from another big market crash. My advice, especially if you are near, at  or in typical retirement age is to at least move as much as you can to U.S. treasury bills and bonds if you stick with a brokerage account. I don't even trust brokerage accounts. FDIC Banks seem about as safe as you can get. If the FDIC fails most of us will be living on bread lines and in soup kitchens. Regardless of the results of this study, I do not understand our cultural orientation towards “slowing down” neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s disease. Anyone who has dealt closely with a loved one suffering from this disease knows that the only humane option would be to speed it up and get their suffering over with faster. Death is better than living with Alzheimer’s. The idea of prolonging the agony is incomprehensible to me. 

Articles like this (and some comments too) that refer to “treatment” are so frustrating. There is no treatment, this disease is awful even if you “slow it down.” It is fatal no matter how you intervene. You might buy yourself a few extra months or years of changing your loved one’s diapers while they rot in delirium, but to what end? 

I wish research would focus more on either prevention, or palliative care. Extending the life span of someone already suffering from Alzheimer’s disease is madness.

If you can’t measure the effect, you really can’t invent a cause.  It’s speculating on the daylight in a windowless room.  
This separates questionable or merely unusual treatment from anything where there’s a chance of measuring something in the blood, on an image, etc.  The latter is how we find how to optimize a treatment.  Once we figure out what might be going on and have a simple way to measure an effect, then we make progress. 
I’m a physics guy, and because of that, get asked about things involving magnets, blinking lights, and in fact, this particular approach.  Mostly by folks trying, again, a certain class of fringy stuff and wanting help with the devices.   But that’s not science, and I happen to include medicine in that sphere.

Climate Remedy
In some polar and alpine regions, the heating is already around +5C. Not 1.5, but 5. In these regions the albedo was strong, historically, with snow and ice reflecting sunlight back into space. As the white stuff disappeared, sunlight is now heating up the dark permafrost, releasing CO2 and CH4, hence contributing to the heating in a nonlinear way. Much of the northern hemisphere  is covered with distressed permafrost.
Reducing CO2 emissions very significantly is needed but impossible in the medium term because the average Earth citizen does not use as much energy as the average citizen in the most developed world, by a factor of at least three. Moreover around 80% of primary energy production is from hydrocarbons.
So what is needed is to deploy massive non carbon energy sources. Hydro, sun and wind can only do that much. That leaves us with nuclear energy, and radical solutions such as displacing energy production to space. Nuclear technologies could be made safe and clean, but that requires a huge investment in research and deployment.
Otherwise, as it is, cataclysmic heating and ocean rise (up to 80 meters in some places) are coming sooner than expected by the experts (who want to please their sponsors, so underestimate the danger).  
Europe wants less energy. Thus moving industry to China (France's CO2 production more than double once Chinese made products are included). The solution then is massive research to avoid going over Jurassic temps (+10C)!

I’m fundamentally in favor of free markets, but many industries and businesses do not function properly without regulation for various reasons. A century ago, financial institutions demonstrated the risks inherent in unregulated financial systems. Jack Kirby was an absolute genius who not only created the most important characters in the Marvel universe, but he also pioneered an artform to draw comic panels in "the Marvel way."

His style energized comic panels with kinetic energy and depth of field based on exaggerated depth of field or vanishing point features that made cityscapes or interplanetary imagery seem cinematic rather than flat. 

His figure drawing, known for pure movement seen through foreshortened limbs and statuesque proportions, took liberties with skeletal or muscular norms to make heroes like Captain America appear more formidable and powerful.

Kirby's signature style has receded from modern comics that now seem flat, static and stiff in comparison to his signature work. 

If I had 1/5 of Kirby's talent to create parallel worlds on a freehand basis I would quit my day job and become a leading illustrator in a medium that has lost its luster.

As a doctor and weightlifter. I take several days or a week off every six weeks or so.  This planned pause (deloading) improves my performance in the gym.

This review reads less like literary criticism than a loyalty oath. A collection of previously published essays served like a reheated lunch, where every anecdote is elevated to insight, and every quip treated as evidence of profundity, as though the mere act of rebinding magazine pieces has transformed them into literature. 

The reviewer seems so enamoured of Gary Shteyngart's persona, the cleverness, the irony, the cultivated self-awareness, that the obvious question never quite gets asked: do these essays amount to anything more than a long record of an intelligent writer performing intelligence? 

One finishes the review with the distinct impression that the book itself is almost beside the point; what is really being celebrated is membership in a cultural club that long ago decided Shteyngart was indispensable and now sees no reason to revisit the verdict.

This performance and article make my point.

Modern British playwrights like Tom Stoppard suffer from the gigantic, literary and historical shadow of William Shakespeare. American playwrights not at all.

After seen few plays by Stoppard, like “Arcadia,” “The Invention of Love,” etc., you get the impression that all what he is trying to do is to measure himself up to Shakespeare. His plays are extremely witty and erudite, with endless references to the Classics, obscure quotations only familiar to specialists, never ending name dropping and ceaseless verbal ping-pong (the last line should be surpassed or outwitted by the next one). All of these make for hard to understand plays with minimal acting. A headache is a side effect, if not a serious complication.

Modern American plays like “A Streetcar Named Desire,” “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?,” “The Price,” etc., are exactly the opposite. A full display of basic human foibles and worse in full rogue energy and tension. No verbal ping-pong here just anger, despair, meanness, jealousy, all kind of passions, delusion and maybe a little bit of love. 

These are the reasons as to why American plays are so successful in London’s venues. As humans, we can all relate to them. For example, whether we recognize it or not, we all have at least, a 10% of Blanche DuBois’s delusion (though she is a pure 100%), that allow us to carry on with the infirmities of daily life.

When I was briefly in Tokyo (just nine days) many years ago, I paid special attention to the local Manga scene. I expected it to be something like the comics world here, which I participated in by creating graphic stories.

I was wrong. Manga, I discovered, was a much broader term referring to a booklet format, printed on inexpensive paper and usually embellished with pictures of some kind -- it often included wonderful drawings, but sometimes was more focused on news, or on useful information about a particular subject. One of the most surprising things was that there were boxes in some subway stations where people getting off a train would put the manga they had finished reading on their commute, so it could be picked up for free and read by another commuter.

Another wonderful bit of trivia about Japanese art: when the French Impressionist movement was getting started, one of their rising stars, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, had a job unpacking imported Asian "china" -- dishes and pottery. He discovered that they were often wrapped in newspaper-like pages of wonderful illustrations -- the Ukyio-e prints of the Edo period had been printed on cheap paper and later discarded to be used as packing materials! He showed them to his artist friends and it had a substantial effect on the aesthetic development of impressionism.

I'm sorry to hear of Tetsuya Chiba's passing. He and the other great Japanese artists, for over a century, have been a great inspiration to American artists.

How, I wondered, could a justly celebrated novelist be so blind to has audience as to waste his time and theirs "preaching to the choir?"  My guess was, and is, that he already written his remarks and decided he would kill a day, pocket his honorarium, and to on to have more fun elsewhere.
